title: Quantitative easing
summary: The Bank of England provides an explanatory overview of its quantitative easing (QE) programme, a monetary policy tool used to lower long-term borrowing costs when Bank Rate is near zero. The UK QE programme purchased a total of £895 billion in bonds (£875bn government gilts, £20bn corporate bonds), with the last expansion announced in November 2020. The Bank is currently in quantitative tightening (QT) mode, having begun bond runoff in February 2022 as inflation is above the 2% target.
key_points: QE involves the Bank buying bonds to push up their prices and bring down long-term interest rates, thereby stimulating economic spending
Total UK QE bond purchases reached £895 billion: £875 billion in UK government bonds (gilts) and £20 billion in UK corporate bonds
The last QE expansion was announced in November 2020; QT began in February 2022
Current policy stance: inflation above 2% target has led to Bank Rate increases, with the Bank actively reducing its bond holdings through QT
QE creates money digitally as central bank reserves to purchase bonds; QT reverses this by letting bonds mature or actively selling them
Research cited by the Bank indicates QE had the largest economic impact during stressed market periods: post-2009, post-Brexit referendum 2016, and spring 2020 pandemic
why_it_matters: This page provides authoritative context on how the Bank of England deploys and withdraws QE as a monetary policy tool. Understanding QE/QT mechanics is essential for fixed income and FX traders, as central bank balance sheet operations directly affect gilt yields, mortgage rates, and overall financial conditions.
macro_context: The page explains the transmission mechanism: QE lowers long-term yields by increasing bond prices, which feeds through to lower mortgage and corporate borrowing costs, stimulating spending and raising inflation. Conversely, QT aims to normalise the balance sheet without directly targeting rates or inflation.
market_structure_context: The page notes that QE 'supports the prices of other financial assets' by channeling bond proceeds into equities and other instruments through asset managers. It also explains how central bank reserves (created digitally) function in the settlement system.

issues_found: Event_type 'monetary_policy_report' is a reasonable approximation but the source is technically an informational/educational explainer page, not a formal monetary policy report. However, given the taxonomy options available, this is the closest valid fit and is defensible.
